evidence.title: K-anonymity decay in multi-turn clinical large language model conversations
evidence.outcome: Cumulative quasi-identifier disclosure across multi-turn LLM prompts eroding anonymity beyond the minimum necessary
evidence.effect: Even with no direct identifiers per turn, 79.9% of patients reached k<5 within a disclosure sequence; median 7 steps under progressive disclosure.
evidence.quote: The re-identification risk emerges not from any non-compliant disclosure but from the steady accumulation of compliant ones.
evidence.sample_unit: simulated patients sampled from 133,262 synthetic patients

commentary.bottom_line: No study has tested whether limiting AI data collection, vendor sharing, or logging to the minimum necessary, with documented justification for each element, reduces patient data exposure. One simulation study shows that re-identification risk can build up across multi-turn AI prompts even when no single prompt contains a direct identifier.

perspectives.view: No study tests the practice, so certainty is rated as no direct evidence. The single available study documents the hazard in 5,000 simulated patients drawn from synthetic records and does not evaluate a minimization policy. Twenty-two sources endorse the practice, but most are guidance or commentary, and the number of endorsements does not substitute for outcome data.

In the simulation, 79.9% of patients reached k<5 within a disclosure sequence, with a median of 7 steps under progressive disclosure, although no turn contained direct identifiers. This suggests that element-by-element review may miss harm that arises from combinations of individually harmless fields. A safeguard that justifies each element separately may leave cumulative exposure unchecked.

The hazard study concerns multi-turn prompts to a language model rather than structured vendor data feeds. Justification lists for each data element fit structured exports more easily than free-text chat. No study reports how organizations apply minimum-necessary review to prompts, logs, or agent tool calls, or how much staff time that review requires.

The endorsements vary in scope and force. Texas SB 1188 bars collecting, storing, or sharing credit score or voter registration status in the electronic health record, which is narrower than a general minimum-necessary rule. The CHAI playbook statement listed concerns validating tool-call outputs rather than data minimization. Most remaining sources are guidance or commentary using should.

commentary.research_gap: No study compares AI deployments with and without per-element minimum-necessary review. Such studies should measure re-identification risk, the volume of data shared with vendors or retained in logs, effects on model performance, and staff time. They should also test whether per-element justification detects cumulative disclosure across prompts and conversation turns.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested the practice, and the one hazard study used synthetic patients and reported no Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy subgroups. Organizations serving these populations therefore have no evidence on whether minimization reduces exposure for their patients. Patients from small communities or less common language groups may carry more distinctive quasi-identifiers, but this has not been studied.
